# Resource-pool config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/pools/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.PoolBlock` (ADR-092 D1), a named set of interchangeable `member`s behind one selection policy. The block label is the pool name.

The pool is the **only** name a consumer references — a worker's `capability_credentials { seat_pool = "..." }` or a tool binding's `seat_pool` attribute — never a member. That attribute keeps its ADR-080 spelling while naming this kind; renaming the consumer-side surface is a later, deliberate step (ADR-092 D10).

A pool lists its members as one `member "<label>" {}` block each (ADR-178 D2). The label names a `member` declared in `.tera/members/<label>.hcl`; a label naming no declared member is refused, and so is the same label twice in one pool. The block says how *this pool* treats the member and takes two attributes and nothing else: `state` and `reason`. Anything that says what the member *is* — `provides`, `seats`, `owner`, `weight` — belongs on its declaration, and writing one inside the block is refused naming `.tera/members/<label>.hcl`. Order carries no meaning.

```hcl
pool "dev-fleet" {
  selection = "least-loaded"

  member "macbook-m4max" {}
  member "local" {
    state  = "draining"
    reason = "dev work off the daemon host"
  }
}
```

A member's **state** in a pool is `open` (the default, and what an unset `state` means), `draining` or `closed` (ADR-178 D1). `open` admits new placements and pinned resumes — runs whose workspace is on that member — within `seats`; `draining` refuses new placements and still admits pinned resumes; `closed` refuses both. No state stops work already running on the member or changes its link, and `seats` keeps its value whatever the state. The state is this pool's alone, so one member can be draining in the dev pools and open in another. `draining` and `closed` require a `reason` saying why, and an empty or whitespace-only one is refused; a `reason` beside an open member is refused, because it would describe a state the member is not in (D4). A pool needs at least one member, and a pool whose members are all `closed` is legal: it is how a pool is turned off while staying declared. **The seat gate admits by a member's state**: a draining or closed member takes no new work from this pool, and a pool with no open member refuses new work with the cause `not-open`, naming each member's state and reason. A resume pinned to a member closed here is refused with the cause `workspace-pin-closed`: the run is held for its machine while the worker's `workspace_hold_deadline` runs, past which it is placed on another machine and its session is lost. A run pinned to the daemon's own host, `local`, is the exception: it is held until the member reopens, with no deadline, because that machine is never away. Reopening the member while the run is held resumes it on its own machine.

The older `members = ["a", "b"]` list is refused in this release, and the refusal prints the `member "a" {}` and `member "b" {}` blocks that replace it, which load to the same members (D8.2). A list that reads a variable is refused naming each variable, and its rewrite writes the variable's current value as the label (D8.3). A pool writing both the list and `member` blocks is refused with its own sentence. `selection` is the policy the seat provider runs at acquire time over live state — the lease ledger, the cooling table and the members' reported meters — skipping members at their ceiling, members marked cooling and members reported `exhausted`; an unrecognised policy is rejected rather than accepted as a name no code implements.

Two policies, and they optimize different things (ADR-092 D9). **`round-robin` is the default** and is what unset means: it rotates over the admissible members, resuming after the one the gate last dispatched onto, which is the floor of the design — a pool of members declaring nothing but `provides` admits dispatches and alternates between them, with no capacity model at all. `least-loaded` picks the least **busy** member, where busy means normalized consumption rather than concurrency: it ranks by status band first (`ok` before `warning`, with `unknown` last but still selectable), then by the *consumption* reading the member's own runtime reported inside that band, and only for a member whose reporter stated no such reading does it fall back to the concurrency signal — which is the **fraction of that member's declared capacity in use**, its live lease count divided by its `weight`, and `weight` defaults to its dispatchable seats. Two hosts declaring 6 and 4 seats therefore take work 6:4 and saturate together, with nothing authored beyond those ceilings; a pool whose members declare equal ceilings ranks exactly as it did when this was a bare lease count. Where that ranking **ties** — which on a pool carrying no meters at all is every decision — it falls through to the same rotation cursor, so an idle pool alternates under either policy instead of packing onto whichever member sorts first. The ranking always wins over the cursor, never the other way round.

Nothing invents a reading it was not given: an absent one is a first-class value, not a zero (ADR-092 D4), which is why a member that reported none is ranked on the signal this policy already had rather than on a synthesized number. A member carrying an `exhausted` meter is not ranked at all — it is not selectable while that report stands (D7) — and a member past its `expires_at` sorts last as a whole, behind every live member, whatever it reported.

**`tera seats list` is where "why was this member skipped" is answered.** A member the policy above will not consider reads `skipped` in its AVAIL column rather than a seat count, its capacity is excluded from the pool's totals and from the WORKERS block's headroom, and the annotation under its row names the condition responsible — the meter id for an exhausted meter, or the cooling window, or the `needs credential` hold. `--json` carries the same fact as `selectable` (`yes` / `no` / `unknown`) with an `unselectable` list beside it. An *expired* member keeps its seat count there, because it is still selectable; the EXPIRY column is where that state is read.

Rotation position lives in the daemon's memory, keyed by pool name — **one cursor per pool, shared by both policies**, so editing `selection` changes how the next member is chosen and never where the pool had got to. It survives a `tera config apply` that leaves the pool declared, and a restart resumes at the pool's first member.

## Example

A minimal `pools`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/pools/example-pool.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

pool "example-pool" {
  member "example-member" {}
}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | block label | Pool name. The value a worker's capability_credentials seat_pool or a tool binding's seat_pool names. |
| `member` | block (list) | no | — | ADR-178 D2 (PLAN-2026-10 member-state, Wave 1) | — | One block per member this pool draws from (ADR-178 D2): member "<label>" {} for an open member, or with state and reason for a member draining or closed in this pool. The label names a member declared in .tera/members/<label>.hcl. The block takes state and reason and nothing else: anything that says what the member IS — provides, seats, owner, weight and the rest — belongs in .tera/members/<label>.hcl, and writing one here is refused naming that file. A pool needs at least one member, and a pool whose members are all closed is legal: it is how a pool is turned off while staying declared. Order carries no meaning: selection is by policy, and rotation is keyed by the pool's name. A label naming no declared member is refused, and so is the same label twice in one pool. The older members list is refused, alone or beside member blocks (see members). The seat gate admits by a member's state: a draining or closed member takes no new work from this pool, and a pool with no open member refuses new work with the cause not-open. A resume pinned to a closed member is refused too, with the cause workspace-pin-closed: the run is held for its machine while the worker's workspace_hold_deadline runs, past which it is placed on another machine and its session is lost. A run pinned to the daemon's own host, local, is the exception: it is held until the member reopens, with no deadline, because that machine is never away. Reopening the member while the run is held resumes it on its own machine. |
| `members` | string[] | no | — | — | — | The older list spelling of this pool's members, which this release refuses (ADR-178 D8.2): a pool writing members = ["a", "b"] is refused, and the refusal prints the member "a" {} and member "b" {} blocks that replace it, which load to the same members. A list that reads a variable is refused naming each variable, and its rewrite writes the variable's current value as the label, since a block label is a literal. A pool writing both members and member blocks is refused with its own sentence. tera config pull writes a list of literals as member blocks, and a list that reads a variable as stored. |
| `selection` | string | no | — | — | — | Policy run at acquire time over live state, skipping members at their ceiling, members marked cooling and members whose runtime reported an exhausted meter. round-robin rotates over the admissible members and is the default; least-loaded picks the least busy member — status band first (ok before warning, unknown last and still selectable), then the consumption reading its reporter stated, then, for a member that reported none, the fraction of its declared capacity in use (live leases divided by the member's weight, which defaults to its dispatchable seats) — and falls through to the same rotation cursor wherever that ranking ties, so an unmetered idle pool alternates under either policy. Both share one cursor per pool, so changing this value never resets rotation. Any other value is rejected. |
| `team_fallback` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Declared team fallback for owned members (ADR-148 D7). Unset or false: a person whose own member in this pool is exhausted has their run PARKED in the capacity park until that member's reported reset, and no team member is drawn for it, however free. It is read only when this pool is the one the dispatch asked for, the head of its overflow chain; a later pool's team_fallback is not read for that draw. true: while EVERY one of that person's own members across the whole chain is exhausted (a provider-reported exhausted meter; a stale report reads unknown and opens nothing), their run may draw a TEAM member (one with no owner) instead, in this pool and then down the chain. It only applies where the work-order type declares no filer {} or worker {} choice for the member's connection; it never draws another person's owned member, and it does not apply to a member that is merely busy, cooling or holding a dead credential. Every draw it makes names both the exhausted owned member(s) and the team member drawn, in the seat.acquired event's fallback_for. |
| `overflow` | string | no | — | — | — | The one other declared pool this pool spills into (ADR-092, the overflow amendment). A draw that finds NO admissible member here for any capacity reason — every member at its ceiling, cooling, exhausted or holding a dead credential — draws from the overflow pool instead, by that pool's own selection policy and meters, and so on down the chain. A spill is recorded as overflow_from on the dispatch and its seat.acquired event. Ownership never spills: a person's draw follows overflow only into a pool where they own a serving member, and an owned member is drawn only for its owner in every pool. Whether the team may be drawn instead is decided by the team_fallback of the pool the dispatch asked for, the head of the chain, and judged over the whole chain; a later pool's team_fallback is not read for that draw. Unset: the pool has no overflow and a draw that finds no admissible member waits, as before. Naming an undeclared pool, or a chain that returns to a pool already in it (this pool included), is refused at load and at plan, naming the chain. seat_pools = ["a", "b"] is not a preference — a dispatch draws one seat from each pool it names — so overflow is where a preference between pools is stated. |
| `interactive_hold` | string | no | — | — | — | How long a seat drawn by an INTERACTIVE dispatch stays leased after that dispatch ends a turn and its run parks at paused:awaiting-interactive-turn (duration; ADR-129 D7). The lease is adopted by a resume inside the window, so a reply does not join the capacity queue; nothing may preempt it. Unset selects 15m, which is a PROPOSAL rather than a measurement. 0 turns the hold off, and the seat then goes back at the park exactly as every other pause reason's does. It is a pool setting because it trades this pool's capacity against a conversation's responsiveness, and a work order type's author cannot know how contended a deployment's pool is. The cost: each turn holds a seat for up to this long whether or not the person comes back. |
| `description` | string | no | — | — | — | Free-form operator prose. |

## `member` block

Repeatable.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | string | yes | — | — | block label | The member this entry draws from: the label of a member declared in .tera/members/<label>.hcl. A reference, not an identity: a label naming no declared member is refused, and so is the same label twice in one pool. |
| `state` | string | no | `open` | ADR-178 D2 (PLAN-2026-10 member-state, Wave 1) | — | This member's state in this pool (ADR-178 D1). open, the default and what unset means, admits new placements and pinned resumes within seats; draining refuses new placements and still admits pinned resumes (runs whose workspace is on this member) within seats; closed refuses both. No state stops, interrupts or reclaims work already running on the member, and none changes its link. The state is this pool's alone: the same member may be draining here and open in another pool. seats keeps its value whatever the state, so reopening is deleting state and reason, or writing state = "open". Any other value is refused. The seat gate admits by the state: a draining or closed member takes no new work from this pool, and a pool with no open member refuses new work with the cause not-open, naming each member's state and reason. A resume pinned to a member closed here is refused with the cause workspace-pin-closed, naming its state and reason: the run is held for its machine while the worker's workspace_hold_deadline runs, past which it is placed on another machine and its session is lost. A run pinned to the daemon's own host, local, is the exception: it is held until the member reopens, with no deadline, because that machine is never away. Reopening the member while the run is held resumes it on its own machine. |
| `reason` | string | no | — | ADR-178 D2 (PLAN-2026-10 member-state, Wave 1) | — | Why this member is draining or closed in this pool (ADR-178 D4). Required when state is draining or closed, and an empty or whitespace-only reason is refused: a member left out of rotation that nobody can explain is the failure this attribute exists to prevent. Refused when state is open or unset, because it would describe a state the member is not in. |
